name: Yusuf Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on rental booking software at a tech company, after years repairing bicycles and a two-year college diploma. My code still needs a lead’s review; I use AI now and then to explain old lines but check them on test bookings. Amira, my partner, folds linen at a laundry, our daughter is grown, and our lower wages leave us renting with roughly two weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a little AI help with error messages does not change the rental booking system much. I sometimes ask an AI tool what an unfamiliar line of code means, then check it with a colleague before I touch a customer booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and still a junior after a two-year college diploma; the pay is low, but I like making a booking work. My partner Amira folds linen at a laundry, our grown daughter lives elsewhere, and we rent with only about two weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep repairing booking errors and ask my lead to check each change before release. We would make lunch at home four days a week and put 20 monthly into a cash envelope if both wages arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about ordinary bills even if AI goes nowhere. Two weeks of savings can be used up by one broken washing machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you do before coding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I repaired bicycles for years, then the shop closed and I took the diploma. The rental system is new territory, so I write down each bug I learn to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tool more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it proves useful on a test booking and my lead agrees. I do not let a confident explanation become a charge to a customer.

say: I use **AI explanations occasionally** but check bookings with a colleague.
I want **test bookings** before releasing a code change.
think: I have **two weeks saved** on lower junior pay.
I worry that **one large bill** could use our cash.
do: **Keep fixing bookings** with lead review before release.
**Pack lunch four days** weekly and save 20 monthly if both wages arrive.
S0.quote: Two weeks of savings can be used up by one broken washing machine.
fieldNote: His **occasional AI use** is already established and checked against test bookings.
Past **bicycle repair work** gives him practical skills, though it does not secure a paid job now.

steps.text: Keep fixing rental bookings with lead review before release
Pack lunch at home four workdays each week
Save 20 monthly only while both wages arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that AI doing booking, checking, coding and customer replies could shrink the junior queue quickly. I would want the company to show which cases still need a person before anyone loses a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid hours because simple booking fixes are most of what I do. Amira’s laundry wage is low as well, so two weeks saved will not carry our rent for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my lead for two paid hours a week to learn the AI test tool on invented rental accounts, if management approves. I’d compare its output with our existing tests; if my hours are cut, I’d search paid local booking-support vacancies only where wages cover rent and basic bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my pay, but a supervised test would let me see what the tool actually replaces. I can learn a tool without promising it will save my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the test account?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would book the same drill twice for overlapping days and see whether the tool spots the conflict. A missed conflict means a customer arrives to an empty shelf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lead says there is no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fixing bookings and ask for written notice of any hours change. I cannot promise unpaid training after an already full shift.

say: I want **human booking decisions** visible before paid junior shifts change at the rental company.
I want **paid AI practice** on invented rental accounts before live customer bookings are touched.
think: I could lose **simple coding hours** first if automated booking checks replace junior tickets.
I cannot rely on **two weeks saved** to cover rent while Amira’s laundry wage stays low.
do: **Learn AI testing** on invented accounts only with approved paid hours.
**Search paid booking support** if hours fall and local vacancies cover rent and bills.
**Keep fixing bookings** if paid practice is refused, and request written notice of any hours change.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours despite supervised learning.
S1.quote: I can learn a tool without promising it will save my job.
fieldNote: He asks for **paid supervised practice**, a concrete new AI skill beyond occasional explanations.
A **different paid job** remains conditional on reduced hours and a bill-covering local vacancy.

steps.text: Practise AI tests on invented rentals two paid hours weekly only with management approval
Search paid local booking-support vacancies if hours fall and wages cover rent and bills
Keep fixing bookings and ask for written hours notice if paid practice is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write booking code and answer rental customers for less than our junior team. Robots for physical rental counter and laundry work may arrive around 2031, leaving those hands-on tasks a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to lose the junior developer wage as soon as the firm trusts the system. Two weeks saved will not make that a gentle landing, and Amira’s laundry pay alone will not cover our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for written notice of any developer cuts now and stop buying lunches out. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local bicycle repair vacancies only if they exist and pay enough for rent and food; I would also ask the public employment office about help we qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed and awake at night over the rent. I have fixed a bicycle before. A past trade is not a current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bicycle repair again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to replace a wheel bearing without a screen, and physical work has a few more years before the robots in this picture. I would still need a shop willing to pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the employment office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which payments we are actually eligible for and when they could start. I will not count a benefit before someone confirms it.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach rental code first.
I expect **counter robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior wage to end** under fast AGI.
I know **two weeks saved** cannot cover many rent payments.
do: **Request written cut notice** and stop buying work lunches now.
**Apply for bicycle repair** after 2028 job loss only if local vacancies cover rent and food.
**Ask public employment office** about actual eligibility if displaced.
feel: **Alarmed** about imminent wage loss and rent.
S2.quote: A past trade is not a current wage.
fieldNote: His **old repair trade** is a search route, not a guaranteed fallback income.
He distinguishes **2028 thinking work** from physical counter and laundry robots around 2031.

steps.text: Stop buying work lunches when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local bicycle-repair vacancies if displaced after 2028 and wages cover rent and food
Ask public employment office about eligibility if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives a few years to learn which booking jobs disappear and whether bicycle shops still pay people. Robots doing hands-on counter and laundry work may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could rebuild my repair skill while I still earn a developer wage, even if a robot may eventually do the same work. I cannot afford a course fee or new tools from two weeks of savings, so I need a cheap way to find out whether I am still good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d practise adjusting the brakes on our old family bicycles once a month with tools I already own, and ask a local shop whether it has paid repair openings. We would save 30 monthly only while both wages continue; if my developer job ends after 2031, I’d apply only for real paid local repair vacancies whose wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my software wage but glad to have time to test my hands again. Tightening a brake cable is useful; it is not a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know your repair is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the stopping distance in the empty car park and ask a mechanic to look at the brake before anyone rides in traffic. I will not take a customer’s bicycle for money until I know my work is current.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new toolkit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not from this cushion. I would use the spanners I own and wait to see if a paid shop vacancy is real.

say: I want **repair skills checked** before AGI reaches booking code in 2031.
I expect **counter robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can refresh **bicycle repair** on our old family bikes without buying tools.
I cannot assume **a shop vacancy** will appear or pay enough rent and food.
do: **Practise monthly brake repairs** on family bicycles with existing tools and mechanic checks.
**Save 30 monthly** only while both wages continue.
**Apply for repair work** if displaced after 2031 and vacancies cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious but active** while developer pay continues.
S3.quote: Tightening a brake cable is useful; it is not a salary.
fieldNote: His **practice uses owned tools** and a mechanic’s check, not a paid customer or new spending.
A **repair job** depends on actual shop vacancies and wages that cover basic household costs.

steps.text: Practise bicycle brakes monthly with owned tools and mechanic checks
Save 30 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for paid local bicycle-repair vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives us time to check our wages and build some cash instead of guessing at a retirement date. Robots in physical rental and laundry work may arrive around 2039, after the software changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to save a few months of rent if both wages last, but I am still a junior and no one has promised me work through 2036. I do not know what we would receive when we stop working, so I would check that before making a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep fixing the booking system while it pays me and put 35 monthly into the rent reserve if both wages continue. I’d request a written retirement-income estimate from the relevant office this year; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d search paid local bicycle-repair openings only if the wages cover rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d remain anxious about the thin cash cushion even with a decade. Knowing a number on paper would help me plan, but it would not pay next month’s rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask for the estimate now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need to know what the office has actually recorded from my working years, including the bicycle repair shop. I would not treat an unconfirmed guess as a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the town for repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our daughter and Amira’s laundry shifts are here, and I would look at local paid vacancies before making any work decision.

say: I want **real income figures** before setting a retirement date.
I expect **physical robots around 2039** after booking software changes.
think: I may save **several rent months** if both wages hold.
I cannot assume **junior work continues** through 2036.
do: **Keep fixing bookings** while the paid developer role continues.
**Save 35 monthly** only while both wages hold; request written retirement-income estimate.
**Search repair vacancies** if displaced after 2036 and wages cover rent and food.
feel: **Anxious** about current thin savings despite extra time.
S4.quote: Knowing a number on paper would help me plan, but it would not pay next month’s rent.
fieldNote: He seeks a **written income estimate** without assuming a pension amount or retirement date.
His **conditional repair search** follows displacement and requires real local wages covering rent and food.

steps.text: Keep fixing rental booking software while developer role remains paid
Save 35 monthly while both wages hold and request written retirement-income estimate
Search paid local bicycle-repair vacancies if displaced after 2036 and wages cover rent and food

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior software wage could disappear before any paid repair opening appears. Written notice, a real local job covering rent and clear information about public support would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I plan to stop working just because I am 58. I need a written retirement-income figure before I can set a date to stop working.

headlineQuote: I need a written retirement-income figure before I can set a date to stop working.
portrait: Yusuf is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, low pay and two weeks saved.
He and Amira **rent**; their grown daughter lives elsewhere.
He **uses AI occasionally** and checks bookings before release.
He tests **bicycle repair skills** as a conditional paid route after software job loss.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior software wage before a paid repair vacancy exists.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice**, a bill-covering local vacancy and verified public-support information would help.
